cash-advance-fee.summary: A cash advance costs more than its upfront fee. In the example, $1,000 with a 5% fee, $3 ATM fee and 30 days of simple interest at 30% APR costs about $77.66 when fees are paid separately. Change the fee treatment and interest convention to match your agreement.
cash-advance-fee.scope: One USD credit-card cash advance with a single full repayment, selected daily simple or compounded interest, explicit day basis and fee treatment. No intervening payments, statement-cycle capitalization, purchase balances, issuer quote, statutory APR or merchant cash advance.

examples.title: Pay fees separately and repay after 30 days
examples.inputs: amount: 1000; fee_rate: 5; minimum_fee: 10; atm_fee: 3; apr: 30; days: 30; day_basis: 365; interest_method: Simple daily; fee_treatment: Pay upfront
steps: Simple interest on $1,000 for 30 days at 30% / 365 is about $24.66.
Cost is about $77.66; principal plus cost is about $1,077.66.
examples.answer: Total modeled cost: $77.66 under these stated assumptions.

examples.title: Finance fees on the same advance
examples.inputs: amount: 1000; fee_rate: 5; minimum_fee: 10; atm_fee: 3; apr: 30; days: 30; day_basis: 365; interest_method: Simple daily; fee_treatment: Finance fees
steps: The same $53 fee is included in the interest-bearing starting balance of $1,053.
Interest is about $25.96; include the fee once in the final cash total.
examples.answer: Total modeled cost: $78.96 under these stated assumptions.

examples.title: Compare daily compounding with simple interest
examples.inputs: amount: 1000; fee_rate: 5; minimum_fee: 10; atm_fee: 3; apr: 30; days: 30; day_basis: 365; interest_method: Daily compound; fee_treatment: Pay upfront
steps: Keep fees separate and change only the approximation to daily compounding.
This is a model comparison, not evidence of your issuer’s capitalization method.
examples.answer: Total modeled cost: $77.95 under these stated assumptions.

examples.title: Zero days isolates the upfront fees
examples.inputs: amount: 1000; fee_rate: 5; minimum_fee: 10; atm_fee: 3; apr: 30; days: 0; day_basis: 365; interest_method: Simple daily; fee_treatment: Pay upfront
steps: Keep the $53 in fees.
With zero accrued days the interest term is zero.
This boundary case is not a promised interest-free withdrawal.
examples.answer: Total modeled cost: $53.00 under these stated assumptions.

questions.question: Does the minimum fee replace the percentage fee?
questions.answer: The advance fee is the larger of the entered percentage charge and minimum fee, then the additional ATM fee is added once.

questions.question: Do the fees themselves accrue interest?
questions.answer: That depends on the agreement. Choose separately paid fees or add both entered fees to the interest-bearing starting balance. Different fee-specific treatment requires a separate calculation.

questions.question: Is the annualized cost an APR quote?
questions.answer: No. It is a simple annualization of the modeled cost relative to cash received. It is not a statutory APR, IRR or effective annual yield, and zero days gives no annualized value.

questions.question: Is the table a minimum-payment schedule?
questions.answer: No. Each row assumes one full repayment on that day and no earlier payment. Use a payoff tool separately for installment budgeting; its rate and balance assumptions must match.

cobra-cost.summary: COBRA premium planning starts with the full plan cost, including the employer contribution. With $200 from the employee, $600 from the employer and a selected 2% administrative charge, the monthly amount is $816 before any entered subsidy. This worksheet estimates premiums, not eligibility or total medical spending.
cobra-cost.scope: Ordinary federal COBRA premium-only worksheet with a 0–2% administrative charge and constant entered monthly subsidy. Matching coverage tier, no eligibility or duration determination, medical spending, state continuation or disability-extension premium model.

examples.title: Combine employee and employer contributions
steps: Full monthly plan cost is $200 + $600 = $800.
The selected 2% administrative charge adds $16.
Monthly amount is $816, or $4,896 over six selected months.
examples.answer: Estimated monthly amount you pay: $816.00 under these stated assumptions.

examples.title: Use an already-known full plan premium
steps: Start with the already-known full $800 premium; do not add employer contributions again.
At 2% and no subsidy, monthly payment is $816.
examples.answer: Estimated monthly amount you pay: $816.00 under these stated assumptions.

examples.title: Model an entered monthly employer subsidy
steps: Keep the $816 premium including the administrative charge.
Subtract the entered $300 monthly subsidy, leaving $516.
Six selected months cost $3,096.
examples.answer: Estimated monthly amount you pay: $516.00 under these stated assumptions.

examples.title: Model a plan with no administrative charge
steps: Select 0% administrative charge on the full $800 premium.
One planning month costs $800; the standard 2% ceiling is not a required fee.
examples.answer: Estimated monthly amount you pay: $800.00 under these stated assumptions.

questions.question: Do I multiply just my old payroll deduction by 1.02?
questions.answer: No. Start with the full plan cost for the same coverage tier, including the amount the employer used to contribute. The ordinary administrative charge can be up to 2%.

questions.question: Does choosing 18 or 36 months mean I qualify?
questions.answer: No. The month input only controls arithmetic. Eligibility, election deadlines, qualifying events and permitted duration require the plan notice and applicable rules.

questions.question: What if the subsidy ends after three months?
questions.answer: Run the subsidized months and remaining unsubsidized months separately, then add the two amounts. This worksheet applies one unchanged subsidy to each selected month.

questions.question: Does this estimate include deductibles or the disability extension?
questions.answer: No. Medical out-of-pocket costs, state continuation and disability-extension premiums are excluded. Certain disability-extension months have different federal limits.
